Given that u=1+x2, which integral is equivalent to ∫x3dx1+x2?

a
12∫u−1/2du
b
12∫(u1/2−u−1/2)du
c
2∫(u1/2−u−1/2)du
d
2∫u1/2du

decision.explanation: Since du=2x dx and x²=u−1, x³ dx=(u−1)du/2. Thus the integral becomes (1/2)∫(u−1)/√u du=(1/2)∫(u^{1/2}−u^{−1/2})du.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Given that $u=1+{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to $\int \frac{{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}?$
after.worked_solution:
Since $u=1+{x}^{2}$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
${x}^{2}=u-1$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\cdot {x}^{2}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (u-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int ({u}^{1/2}-{u}^{-1/2})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Given that $u=1+{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to $\int \frac{{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}?$
content.worked_solution:
Since $u=1+{x}^{2}$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
${x}^{2}=u-1$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\cdot {x}^{2}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (u-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int ({u}^{1/2}-{u}^{-1/2})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since u=2x+1, x=(u−1)/2 and dx=du/2. Therefore ∫x∛(2x+1)dx=(1/4)∫(u−1)u^{1/3}du=(1/4)∫(u^{4/3}−u^{1/3})du, which is option b.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given that $u=2x+1$, which integral is equivalent to $\int x\sqrt[3]{2x+1}\,\text{d}x?$
after.worked_solution:
Since $u=2x+1$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{1}{2}(u-1).$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt[3]{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(u-1)(\sqrt[3]{u})(\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int (u-1)({u}^{1/3})\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int ({u}^{4/3}-{u}^{1/3})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Given that $u=2x+1$, which integral is equivalent to $\int x\sqrt[3]{2x+1}\,\text{d}x?$
content.worked_solution:
Since $u=2x+1$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{1}{2}(u-1).$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt[3]{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(u-1)(\sqrt[3]{u})(\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int (u-1)({u}^{1/3})\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int ({u}^{4/3}-{u}^{1/3})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $u=3-2{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to ${\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x?$
after.worked_solution:
Since $u=3-2{x}^{2}$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4x\,⟹\,-\frac{\text{d}u}{4}=x\text{d}x.
$$

We also note that ${x}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(3-u).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $1$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{2}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(3-u)\sqrt{u}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}u}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{3}(3-u)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$
